stops.name: Sapporo Clock Tower
stops.story: This wooden hall began as the drill hall of Sapporo Agricultural College. Step inside to see how a new frontier city took shape; time your visit near the hour for the clock chime.

stops.name: Nijo Market
stops.story: Sapporo grew around the fishing and farming communities of the Ishikari region. Nijo Market still makes a lively morning stop for seafood, produce, and a close look at Hokkaido ingredients. Stall hours vary.

photo.alt: Seafood stalls at Sapporo Nijo Market

stops.name: Sapporo TV Tower
stops.story: From the observation deck, Odori Park reads as a long green axis through central Sapporo, with the city and distant mountains beyond it. Check visibility before paying for the view.

photo.alt: View of Odori Park from Sapporo TV Tower

stops.name: Odori Park
stops.story: Odori is both a downtown park and a civic stage. Walk its broad blocks to see fountains, flower beds, and seasonal events; the character changes with the festival calendar.

photo.alt: Odori Park in central Sapporo

stops.name: Ganso Sapporo Ramen Yokocho
stops.story: This compact Susukino alley is known for small ramen counters serving Sapporo-style miso bowls. Pick a shop that is open when you arrive, since hours and queues differ.

stops.name: Sendai Asaichi (Morning Market)
stops.address: Sendai Asaichi, Chuo, Aoba Ward, Sendai, Japan
stops.story: This compact market is known as the city kitchen: look for Sanriku seafood, seasonal Miyagi produce, breakfast bowls, and freshly fried croquettes. The official visitor guide places it five minutes from Sendai Station’s west exit. Go in the morning, check the day before travelling, and expect individual stalls to set their own hours; the guide lists Sundays and national holidays as closure days.

coordinates.precision: OSM mapped market point; not a specific stall entrance

photo.alt: Sendai Asaichi market and nearby city buildings

stops.name: Zuihoden Mausoleum
stops.address: 23-2 Otamayashita, Aoba Ward, Sendai, Miyagi 980-0814, Japan
stops.story: Date Masamune, founder of the Sendai domain, chose this hillside as his final resting place. The richly colored mausoleum sits among cedar trees, so the visit shifts from ornate Momoyama-style detail to a quiet, shaded approach. Allow 45 to 60 minutes. The official access notes about 80 steep steps to reception and around 30 more across the grounds; visitors who need step-free access should check with the venue before making this a fixed stop. Loople’s stop is Zuihoden-mae, followed by a walk of about seven minutes.

coordinates.precision: Commons geotagged camera point within the precinct, not the ticket entrance

photo.alt: Colorfully decorated Zuihoden Mausoleum among cedar trees

stops.name: Sendai City Museum
stops.address: 26 Kawauchi, Aoba Ward, Sendai, Miyagi 980-0862, Japan
stops.story: The museum stands on the former Sannomaru grounds of Sendai Castle and holds roughly 100,000 objects connected with the Date family and the region. Look for the story behind Date Masamune’s black-lacquered armor and the Keicho-era mission to Europe. The permanent display changes seasonally, and the armor is shown only during selected periods, so check the current exhibition before choosing this as the day’s anchor. Allow about one to one and a half hours. The Loople stop is shared with Sendai International Center.

coordinates.precision: OSM mapped museum point; entrance location may differ

photo.alt: Exterior of Sendai City Museum

stops.name: Sendai Castle Site and Kenbunkan
stops.address: Sendai Castle Site, Aoba-yama, Aoba Ward, Sendai, Japan
stops.story: The Honmaru occupied a hill about 130 metres above the city. From the open castle site, the view reaches across Sendai and, on clear days, toward the Pacific; the equestrian statue of Date Masamune is the landmark most visitors look for. Before walking the grounds, step into Kenbunkan, the free historical information facility, for models and displays that make the stone walls and layout easier to read. Allow about 45 to 60 minutes for the museum and castle-site walk together. Loople stops at Sendai Castle Site.

coordinates.precision: OSM mapped equestrian statue point on the castle site; not a bus stop

photo.credit: Gustave67 (photograph of work by Tōru Komuro)
photo.alt: Equestrian statue of Date Masamune at the Sendai Castle Site

stops.name: Jozenji-dori Avenue
stops.address: Jozenji-dori Avenue, Kokubuncho, Aoba Ward, Sendai, Japan
stops.story: End beneath the zelkova canopy on the central promenade. The avenue takes its name from a temple that no longer stands, linking the modern city back to Sendai’s founding era. In spring and summer the branches make a green tunnel; autumn turns the leaves gold, and in winter the Pageant of Starlight lights the trees. Sculptures and shops give the walk a distinctly urban feel. Loople serves the Jozenji-dori Avenue / City Hall stop. The avenue is public space, so time needed depends on how long you choose to wander.

photo.alt: A view from the former keep site at Fukuoka Castle

stops.name: Ohori Park
stops.address: Ohori Park, Ohorikoen, Chuo, Fukuoka, Japan
stops.story: The loop around the water is a calm counterpoint to Hakata’s busy streets. Take the path slowly and leave time for the Japanese garden if it is open.

photo.alt: The lake and walking paths at Ohori Park in Fukuoka

stops.name: Tenjin yatai area
stops.address: Tenjin yatai area, Tenjin, Chuo, Fukuoka, Japan
stops.story: If stalls are operating, finish with a meal at a yatai. Each stall is independent and may close for weather or a day off; bring a flexible dinner plan.

coordinates.precision: OSM food-stall point in the Tenjin yatai area

photo.alt: A yatai food stall on Watanabe-dori in Tenjin, Fukuoka

routes.title: Naha: Ryukyu heritage to the night market streets
routes.introduction: Start on the hill at Shuri, then descend toward Tsuboya’s pottery lanes and the city’s covered markets. Keep the last stop flexible for the day’s market hours and street activity.

stops.name: Shurijo Castle Park
stops.address: Shurijo Castle Park, Shuri, Naha, Japan
stops.story: Follow the gates and ramparts through the former Ryukyu royal precinct. Restoration and visitor routes continue to evolve; check the official park update for the areas open on your date.

photo.alt: The red gate and walls of Shurijo Castle in Naha

stops.name: Tsuboya Yachimun Street
stops.address: Tsuboya Yachimun Street, Tsuboya, Naha, Japan
stops.story: Stone-paved lanes, kilns and small galleries tell the story of Okinawan pottery. Browse respectfully; many workshops are working spaces with their own opening hours.

photo.alt: Historic pottery shops along Tsuboya Yachimun Street

stops.name: Makishi Public Market
stops.address: Makishi Public Market, Matsuo, Naha, Japan
stops.story: Explore the market floors and the surrounding arcade for Okinawan ingredients and everyday food culture. Check current floor access and vendor hours before planning a meal here.

photo.alt: The colorful stalls inside Makishi Public Market

stops.name: Kokusai-dori & Heiwa-dori
stops.address: Kokusai-dori & Heiwa-dori, Naha city centre, Japan
stops.story: Finish among the central shopping streets and covered lanes. The neighbourhood is liveliest later in the day; Sundays may bring pedestrian-only activity on parts of the main street.

photo.alt: Kokusai-dori shopping street in central Naha
